answer: Four objects form the chain. pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> turns supervision on for that port and bin: set tca-supervision true and data-supervision true; show also lists supported-parameters (max 100 elements). pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> carries the limits for that instance: add or set with low-threshold and high-threshold, values are Number (uint64, int64, decimal64), na or not-supported, default na. pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter> holds the per-type values and shows default-low-threshold, default-high-threshold, min-value and max-value, for example set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200. pm-resource-<resource> gates real-time-supervision (default true) and show pm displays the counters. direction defaults to all, location defaults to all.

Create the key first: add ntp-key-<key-id> key-type <sha-1|aes-cmac|sha-256|md5> key-value <string 8..40> is-trusted true. key-id range is 1..65534 and is-trusted defaults to false. Then add ntp-server-<ip-address> auth-key-id <id>, where ip-address may be IPv4, IPv6 or a DNS name; origin is dhcp or manual (default manual), admin-state defaults to unlock, alarm-report-control defaults to allowed. Enable globally with set ntp ntp-enabled true ntp-auth-enabled true; ntp-enabled defaults to true, ntp-auth-enabled defaults to false, assignment-method is manual, dhcp or both (default both). To check it works: show ntp ntp-active-server, then show ntp-server-status-<ip-address> for auth-status (ok, yes, bad, none), reach (377 means every recent probe was answered), stratum, offset, jitter, delay, poll and condition. show clock time-source reads ntp once synchronised.

They address different things. protection-switch moves traffic on a protection group: protection-switch [-f] [operation-type=]<value> [switch-target=]<value> [protection-group=]<value>, with operation-type force, lockout, manual or release. switch-target is not needed for release and lockout. Example: protection-switch protection-group-test operation-type=force switch-target=protection. manual-switchover moves the controller: manual-switchover [-f] [resource=]<AID>, for example manual-switchover card-1-3 on a G42, card-1-5 on a G32, card-1-12 on a G34c. It prompts that the controller will switch over and the connection to the management interface will be lost, so confirm at the prompt or use -f. Both are Operational mode only. Check show controller-card redundancy-status and redundancy-standby-status before switching a controller.

set-time is only applicable when time-source is manual, that is when NTP is not enabled, so an active NTP source is what rejects it. Run show clock: time-source is ntp or manual (default manual), and it also gives current-time, universal-time, timezone, uptime, DST-active and last-time-jump in the form <time1> to <time2> (jumps under 10 seconds are ignored). Check show ntp for ntp-enabled and ntp-active-server, and show ntp-server-status-<ip-address> for reach, stratum, offset and auth-status. If you must set it by hand, first set ntp ntp-enabled false, then set-time 2021-02-06T11:16:58Z, ISO 8601 derived format with Z for UTC or +/-hh:mm for another zone. The time command shows the system time in the configured timezone, not the one used in set-time.

show ne gives the identity: ne-id, ne-name (default 1830 GX), ne-type (G30 or G40), node-type (ILA, OADM, XPDR), l0-mode-op, ne-site, ne-location, clli, contact, node-controller-chassis-name (default 1), plus recover-mode, recover-mode-reason, equipment-discovery-ready and alarm-report-ready. For contents, show chassis, show slot (supported-type, installed-type, oper-state, avail-state, current-equipment), show card-<name> and show inventory (actual-type, serial-number, clei, part-number, PON, hardware-version, fw-status). The cost is in restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>]: type warm is the default and is non service affecting, with connectivity back within five minutes; cold reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting; shutdown gracefully shuts the card down. With no resource-id the active controller card is restarted. show card resources lists sub-components.

Slot 2 of chassis 1 is slot-1-2: show slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name> gives AID, supported-type, installed-type, oper-state, avail-state and current-equipment. The card in it is card-1-2, created with add card-<name> required-type <value> chassis-name <value> slot-name <value>, optionally subslot-name for sub-cards (subslot-name can only be set at creation). Under the card hang port objects, port-<card-name>-<port-name>, which are system-managed and cannot be manually deleted. In a pluggable cage you add tom-<card-name>-<port-name> required-type <CFP2-DCO|OSFP|QSFP28|QSFPDD|QSFPDD-ZR|QSFPPLUS|SFP|SFPPLUS>; the tributary port termination point is auto-created with the TOM and auto-deleted with it. The pluggable FRU data is show inventory-<card-name>-<port-name>, for example show inventory-1-3-1, giving actual-type, actual-subtype, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, number-of-lanes, vendor-compliance-code and fw-status.

Capability lives in the supported-* objects, keyed by card-type rather than by the installed instance. show supported-card-<card-type> gives supported-subtype, supported-card-mode and default-card-mode, card-width (na, single-slot, double-slot, half-slot, triple-slot), card-height in RUs, category (controller, line-card, fan, power-supply, other, carrier-card, blank), max-power-draw, is-field-replaceable, console-port-support and supported-bands. show supported-port-<card-type>/<port-name> gives port-type, direction, default-tom and allows-auto-migration; show supported-tom-<card-type>/<port-name>/<tom-type>/<tom-subtype-group> gives supported-subtype, supported-phy-modes and default-phy-mode; show supported-slot-<chassis-type>/<slot-name> gives possible-card-types. What the fitted unit is doing is show card-<name>: required-type, required-subtype, card-mode, power-profile, category, last-reboot-reason, admin-state, oper-state and avail-state.

The parents must exist first. add ospf-instance-<instance-id> router-id <dotted-quad>, instance-id 0..255, version ospfv2 (default) or ospfv3, router-id-mode manual or use-loopback (default use-loopback, which requires an ipv4 LO-MGMT address). Then add ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>; the OSPF instance must be created before the area, ospf-area-type is normal. Then add ospf-interface-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>; instance and area must both be present. Its defaults are enable true, hello-interval 10 s (1..32767), router-dead-interval 40 s (4..65535), ospf-cost 10, priority 1, ospf-if-routing auto. Progress is in show ospf-neighbor-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<router-id>: state moves down, init, 2-way, exstart, exchange, loading, full, with role drother, dr, bdr or ptp. The neighbor is deleted when the OSPF interface is down, and both NEs need instance, area and interface with the DCN bridges connected.

Per card use show software-load-<location-id>/<swload-state>, where location-id is <chassis-id>-<slot-id> and swload-state is active, inactive or installable, for example show software-load-1-5/active. It reports swload-version, swload-manifest, swload-prepared, swload-status, swload-activation-type (direct, warmstart, coldstart), swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label and swload-pkg-type. The individual pieces are show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name> with state (installed, not-installed, installation-failed, unknown; default unknown), version and description, and below them show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name>, for example show sw-subcomponent-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg/ztp.deb. The bundled firmware is show packaged-fw-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> with fw-version; compare it with show current-fw, which gives fw-version, expected-fw-version and fw-status.

The per-port switch is lldp-admin-status, present on comm-eth-<card-name>-<port-name> and on ethernet: tx-only, rx-only, tx-and-rx or disabled, default disabled, for example set comm-eth-1-5-ETH1 lldp-admin-status tx-and-rx. On ethernet there are also lldp-ingress-mode and lldp-egress-mode (disabled, snoop, drop, snoop-and-drop, default disabled). show lldp-local-info-<lldp-port> shows what the node sends: chassis-id is the chassis serial number, port-id the port AID, system-name the NE name. show lldp-port-statistics-<lldp-port>/ingress gives the counts: total-frames-out proves transmission, total-frames-in reception, plus total-discarded-frames, error-frames, total-discarded-tlvs and total-ageouts, all defaulting to 0. Egress direction is not supported and all counters freeze while lldp-admin-status is disabled. Peers appear in show lldp-neighbor-<lldp-port>/ingress; the global show lldp hold-on-timer defaults to 900 seconds.

show slot lists every position as slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name> with AID, supported-type, installed-type (blank when nothing is fitted), oper-state, avail-state and current-equipment. show inventory-<chassis-name>-<slot-name> gives the FRU record of whatever is installed: actual-type, actual-subtype, hardware-version, sw-support-revision (default 0), PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date, insertion-date, number-of-lanes and fw-status, which is not-applicable, current, not-current or unavailable (default not-applicable). The running level per firmware image is show current-fw-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>/<fw-name> with fw-version, expected-fw-version and fw-status (current, not-current, unavailable; default unavailable), for example current-fw-1-1/CORE_BOOT 0x20 against expected 0x28 shows not-current.

show manifest lists the downloaded manifest files, and show manifest-<manifest-file> gives manifest-signature, downloaded-on (YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ) and information. The contents are show manifest-component-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<name>, giving state, version and description; state is where you see whether each piece got installed, with values installed, not-installed, installation-failed or unknown (default unknown). show manifest-firmware-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> gives the bundled fw-version, and show fru-info-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type> gives the packaged FRU information for an equipment-type. Once the package is a software load on a card, the equivalent views are show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name> and show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name>, with the same installed / not-installed / installation-failed / unknown states.

Both come from per resource-type profiles. Alarm severity: set alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location> severity <critical|event|major|minor|not-reported|warning>, with direction na, ingress or egress and location na, near-end or far-end; show also returns service-affecting (indeterminate, sa, nsa, sa-nsa). set alarm-severity-profile <profile-entry> severity <value> edits the same profile, which is system-managed and cannot be manually deleted. PM: set pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> default-data-supervision <true|false> default-tca-supervision <true|false> decides what newly created resources of that type get. Globally, set pm-profile global-data-supervision auto-enabled or manual (default manual, meaning supervision is controlled per pm-profile-entry or per pm-control-entry). Default threshold values live in pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/... as default-low-threshold and default-high-threshold.

ipsec-spd-entry-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name> makes that decision: action is protect, bypass or discard, default protect. It also carries the mandatory priority (uint8, used to give precedence between SPD entries), ipsec-protocol ESP, mode tunnel or transport (default tunnel), esn (default true), anti-replay-window 32..1024 (default 64, only when action is protect) and dynamic-ts (default disabled). Underneath hangs ipsec-traffic-selector-<local-instance>/<peer>/<spd-entry>/<ts-name> with next-layer-protocol (any = 0, opaque = 255, or a number 0..255; default any), and under each selector local-subnet and remote-subnet keyed .../<prefix>, and local-ports and remote-ports keyed .../<start>/<stop>. The SPD entries for a peer are grouped by security-policy-database-<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name>, whose associated-secure-entity lists them.

trusted-certificate-<id> is the CA you trust: the X509v3 CA root and intermediate certificates trusted by the system. local-certificate-<id> is this node's own identity, the end-entity certificate representing one of the various secure application identities; its used-by attribute lists the secure-applications and ikev2-peers presently using it, and trust-chain lists the trusted certificates above it. peer-certificate-<id> is the far end: the trusted remote peer end-entity certificate for the L1 encryption secure application, and it uniquely carries white-listed, which is true when it was imported with no trust chain. The fourth name, certificate, is not a per-certificate object: show certificates lists all managed local, trusted and peer certificates, show certificate-revocation lists revocations, and clear certificate type=<trusted|local|peer> id=<id> removes one.

It goes on with import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>], Operational mode only, where certificate type is trusted-certificate, local-certificate or peer-certificate. Example: import-certificate local-certificate certificate-name=local-cert-1 <string in PEM format> <passphrase>. The -i flag also imports intermediate certificates present in a PEM bundle, or those referenced by the AIA extension; root certificates must be installed individually, and with no certificate-name the name is derived from the topmost issuer CN plus a numeric suffix, for example trusted-certificate-Nokia-1. Certificates can also arrive by the download mechanism in PKCS#12 or PKCS#7 secure bundles. To take one off: clear [-f] certificate type=<trusted|local|peer> id=<id>, and the id must match a currently installed but unused certificate. Bulk types are purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused and purge-peer-unused. display-cert shows the details.

access-rule-<access-rule-list-name>/<access-rule-name> is the one that permits or denies: action permit or deny is mandatory when the rule is created, and the match is narrowed by module-name (default *), path (XPath of a data node, notification, RPC or an external command; default *), attribute and attribute-value (leaf-lists, max 10 entries of up to 64 chars) and operation (bits create, read, update, delete, execute; default * for all). access-rule-list-<name> is the grouping and ordering object: the list is processed in order given by sequence-id, and user-group names which user-groups it applies to (default *, all). sw-control-rule-<service-name> has nothing to do with traffic: it overrides what happens when a software service fails, with fail-action default-action, ignore or system-restart. access-control-list is read-only, show access-control-list. Packet filtering proper is acl and ace.

Ordering is by sequence-id and lower number ids are processed first, so the rule with the lower sequence-id takes effect. sequence-id is a uint16, applied both to each access-rule within its list and to the access-rule-list itself; if you do not provide one it is set to the currently used latest id plus 1, so the entry goes to the end of the list. The id can be changed over the lifetime of the list to re-sort entries. On access-rule-list-<name>, user-group is a leaf-list of user-group names or the match-all default *, and a maximum of 20 user-groups can be referenced. The system supports a maximum of 500 access-rules across all access-rule-lists. Both commands run in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

The trap community string is not in snmp-community; the guide states the trap-community-string is located in the snmp-target object. Set it with add snmp-target-<target-name> snmpv3-user <value> target-address <value> trap-community-string <value>, or set snmp-target-<target-name> trap-community-string <value>. It is a string of 0..32 characters and defaults to infinera, which is what a receiver rejects if it was never changed. The rest of the target: snmp-version v2c (default) or v3, snmpv3-user only when the version is v3, target-address as IPv4/IPv6 or hostname, target-port 0..65535 default 162, target-transport udp, enabled default true. snmp-community-<name> holds only read access strings: community-string 1..32 chars, community-string-access read-only, enabled default true. Global control is set snmp enabled <true|false> and port (1..65535, default 161).

external-fiber-connection is the one written by something other than you: the guide states it is set autonomously by TNMS, and although it can be configured manually that is not recommended. It represents a physical link between ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or within one NE in disaggregated configurations, addressed as external-fiber-connection-<name> with src-node-id, src-card-name, src-port-name, dst-node-id, dst-card-name, dst-port-name, fiber-connection-type one-way or two-way (default two-way) and scope general-purpose or cable-id (default general-purpose; cable-id is required for CableID path verification). fiber-connection-<name> is the user-provisioned link between two distinct ports or sub-ports in the same NE, with src-port, dst-port and fiber-connection-type. supporting-fiber-connection-<name> is show only, returning the fiber-connection-list for an entity.

For the node's own address use ipv4-address: add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>, for example add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0 or add ipv4-address-1-AUX-1/200.20.20.186 netmask '255.255.240.0'. show returns netmask and origin (static, dhcp, auto-config; default static). The other two are read-only LLDP views, not configuration. management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> reports the management address advertised by the remote system seen on that port, with if-subtype, if-id and address-oid. management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address> reports the management address this node advertises in its own LLDP, with if-subtype unknown, if-index or system-port-number. Neither assigns an address to an interface.

The stated pre-condition on ipv4-address is that a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. Check show interface-<if-name>: ipv4-address-assignment-method is static or dhcp (default static) and ipv4-enabled is true or false (default true); use set interface-<if-name> ipv4-address-assignment-method static before retrying. The address is validated too: addresses beginning with 0 (current network), 127 (loopback) or 224 up to 255 (broadcast, multicast, experimental) are disallowed, and only valid netmasks are accepted. To see which interfaces are available, type ? after ipv4-address- and the system displays the object completion options, or run show interface, which lists if-name, if-type, supporting-port, backup-port, protection-mode, vrf, admin-state, oper-state and avail-state.

show route is the consolidated view of every route in use: route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> lists system routes from various sources, with source-protocol naming the origin (OSPF, BGP, static and so on) and special-next-hop none, blackhole or unreachable (default none). The containers are show rib-<rib-name>, with vrf and address-family ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast; for each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family. show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> gives next-hop-address, and show routing gives overall routing information. Hand-typed routes are added with add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> next-hop-address <ip> [interface <name>] [distance <1..255, default 1>] [advertised <true|false, default false>] [special-next-hop blackhole], origin manual or dhcp (default manual); ipv6-static-route is the v6 equivalent.

local-ports and remote-ports belong to the IPsec tunnel: both are Layer 4 port ranges inside a traffic selector. add local-ports-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop>, and remote-ports uses the same key, for example add local-ports-ipsec/GX1/dns/ts1/53/53 or add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/all. start may be all, opaque or a port number; stop defaults to 0 and 0 is only accepted when start is all or opaque. connection-ports is the connectivity object: show connection-ports-<degree-number>/<index> maps a degree to its dwdm-line port on an RD or ILAx card, which also creates the OMS of that port. degree-number is 1..20 and must not exceed max-degrees; index is 1..2 but is always 1 in 1830 GX because dwdm-line ports are bidirectional.

take-snapshot makes the copy: take-snapshot [[db-passphrase=]<value>] [[db-instance=]<value>] [[description=]<value>], storing the current configuration database in a local backup slot. db-instance is temp (default, used for manual backup and restore), manual (permanent storage), the automatic onehour, oneday and oneweek, or rollback; type is db-backup (default) or system-backup. It is refused unless a db-passphrase is configured, globally with set security-policies db-passphrase or on the command; it needs a minimum of 40 characters, no dictionary words, Z85 character set. Retaking an existing instance such as oneweek overwrites it. activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>] puts it back; the pre-condition is that a snapshot must have been taken, and sanity-check-override defaults to false. show database and show database-<database-type> list what exists, with backup-time, description, ne-name and database-state.
